summary: Raises questions about the ARPANET topology shown in RFC 597, in particular how well connected some nodes are. RFC 613 replies to it.

plainLanguage.summary: This short memo asks two questions about the ARPANET's network layout. It considers the effects of a failed connection and of a failed IMP.

subtitle: Two questions about link counts and regional loops on an ARPANET map.

tldr.problem: A map of the November 1973 ARPANET raised questions about how its network connections were arranged.
tldr.mechanism: The author asks whether an IMP should have at most three connections and whether more regions should be connected in loops.
tldr.outcome: The RFC asks questions rather than setting requirements. The unit metadata says it updates RFC 597 and was updated by RFC 613.

today: RFC 603 has status listed as Unknown and is a historical discussion of an ARPANET map. The unit metadata says it updates RFC 597 and was updated by RFC 613.

sections.title: The Map Under Discussion
sections.content:
J. D. Burchfiel says he has several questions about the November 1973 ARPANET topographical map. RFC 603 is a short response to the host-status map in RFC 597.

The memo presents two questions about network connections. It does not define a protocol or establish rules for network design.
sections.plainLanguage: The author looked at an ARPANET map and raised two questions about how its connections were arranged. The memo does not prescribe a design.

sections.title: How Many Connections Should an IMP Have?
sections.content: The first question concerns AMES, described as four-connected. If its IMP fails, four network connections will go down. The author asks whether there is an aim for IMPs to have no more than three connections.
sections.plainLanguage: The author asks whether an IMP should have a limit on how many connections it serves. The example is AMES, where an IMP failure affects four connections.

sections.title: Loops Between Network Areas
sections.content:
The seven IMPs in the Washington area are arranged in a loop. The author notes that local communication can continue if one connection fails, and says this may help prepare for area routing.

He contrasts this with a break between MIT-IPC and MIT-MAC, which he says would require a 12-hop route through Washington. He suggests a short connection between Harvard and Lincoln Labs and asks whether Boston, San Francisco and Los Angeles might also be arranged in loops.
sections.plainLanguage: The author asks whether more regions should have loops like Washington's. He notes that another connection could avoid a long route through Washington after a break.

references.text: RFC 597, Host Status, the map discussed by this memo.
